title: Vanity of vanities
hook: vanity of vanities, all is vanity, a word meaning breath or vapor (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
tomorrow: is 'no new thing under the sun' bad news, or a comfort?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Confucius's life in decades, ending with a heart that can be trusted. My decades. Now a new book from a different shelf, and a very different voice: a king who tried everything.

Bigger house, better job, one more trip: the next thing always promises to be the one that lasts. The book of Ecclesiastes is told by a man the King James Bible calls the Preacher, a king in Jerusalem, who runs an experiment on his own life. "I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards," he says. Then gardens, pools, servants, silver and gold, singers. Whatever his eyes wanted, he didn't keep from them. Then he stands back and looks at all of it.
screen: `THE NEXT THING THAT LASTS.` → `I BUILDED ME HOUSES.` → `HE LOOKS AT ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: "And, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun." Vanity is the King James word. The Hebrew is hevel, and a standard Hebrew dictionary gives its first meaning as vapor, or breath. It's even Abel's name in Genesis, the brother whose life was brief. So when the book opens, "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity," it isn't calling life worthless. Hear it as: breath of breaths, all is breath. Brief. Real while it lasts, and impossible to hold. Now the turn. Qoheleth, as the Preacher is called in Hebrew, doesn't stop at the empty shelves. Again and again he comes back to the same counsel: there's nothing better than to eat and drink and find good in your work, and that too, he says, is from the hand of God. In some Jewish communities the whole book is read aloud at Sukkot, the harvest festival kept in flimsy huts open to the sky. The teaching, plainly: in this book of the Hebrew Bible, life is hevel, a breath. You can't grasp it. You can receive it, like bread while it's still warm.
screen: `ALL WAS VANITY.` · `HEVEL: BREATH, VAPOR.` · `ABEL'S NAME, A BRIEF LIFE.` · `EAT, DRINK: FROM THE HAND OF GOD.` · then, large: `BREATH, VAPOUR.`

segments.voice: If there's a window, a mirror or a cold glass nearby, breathe on it gently and watch the cloud spread, then fade. Do it again, slowly, a few times. That's hevel: real for a moment, and already leaving.
Vanity of vanities: in Hebrew, hevel of hevels. Breath of breaths, the line that opens the book and comes back near its end.
Hold onto this: breath, vapour, because brief isn't the same as worthless; it's a reason to taste it. Until tomorrow.
